evidence.quote: More than 256,000 people in Djibouti, around 25 per cent of the population, are likely to face crisis or emergency level hunger over the coming months. Nearly 70 per cent of their population, over 21,000 people, have been classified under the crisis level or above.

Despite recurrent droughts and limited resources, Djibouti has maintained a long-standing open-door policy and has been recognized as a regional leader in implementing the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework (CRRF). The Government has taken bold steps to include refugees in national systems such as education, health care, and employment.

Police regularly use violence to disperse unauthorized protests and arrest participants, and local human rights groups that work on politically sensitive matters cannot operate freely, face difficulties in registering with the authorities, and are subject to government harassment.

A constitutional amendment was passed in 2025 that allowed him to run again. The amendment, which was ratified by parliament on 2 November 2025, was criticised by the president of the Djiboutian League for Human Rights, Omar Ali Ewado, stating that the change prepared Djibouti for a presidency for life under Guelleh.

Djibouti hosts approximately 32,000 people forced to flee, including over 23,000 refugees and 8,000 asylum-seekers, primarily from Somalia, Ethiopia, and Yemen. Around 85% reside in refugee villages such as Ali Addeh, Holl-Holl, and Markazi.

Presidential elections were held in Djibouti on 10 April 2026, and incumbent fifth term president Ismail Omar Guelleh was re-elected to a sixth term, having been president since 1999. Most of the opposition parties either boycotted the election or decided to support Guelleh.

Despite recurrent droughts and limited resources, Djibouti has maintained a long-standing open-door policy and has been recognized as a regional leader in implementing the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework (CRRF). The Government has taken bold steps to include refugees in national systems such as education, health care, and employment.
The opposition's ability to operate is severely constrained, and journalists and activists who air criticism of Guelleh or the UMP are regularly harassed or arrested.
